title: Circulatory effects of the ultra-short-acting β1-Adrenoceptor antagonist landiolol in critically ill patients
summary:
Background
In severely ill patients in the intensive care unit, a sudden irregular heart rhythm can often occur. This condition may further strain the circulation and is associated with a worse overall outcome. Medications that slow down the heart rate are commonly used for treatment, but their effects on the circulation in routine intensive care practice are not yet fully understood.

Research Question
The aim of this study is to investigate how a short-acting medication used to slow the heart rate affects the circulation of critically ill patients and how safe its use is in everyday clinical practice.

Methods
In this study, adult patients in the intensive care unit who develop a new irregular heart rhythm and in whom treatment with the medication is started will be included. Circulatory function will be measured before and during treatment using a specialized monitoring system that records various heart and circulation parameters. In addition, clinical parameters such as the need for circulation-supporting medications, laboratory values, and any adjustments in treatment will be documented.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Critically ill patients admitted to the intensive care unit with new-onset tachyarrhythmia (in particular atrial fibrillation) with a clinical indication for rate control using landiolol as part of routine clinical care.

- Presence of a clinical indication for advanced hemodynamic monitoring using transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO® system), including the requirement for central venous access for this purpose.

- Ability to provide informed consent or presence of appropriate consent/legal representation.
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients under the age of 18 years.

- Pregnant or breastfeeding women.

- Known contraindications to beta-blockers (e.g., high-grade atrioventricular block without pacemaker, clinically relevant bradycardia).

- Severe cardiogenic shock or hemodynamic instability in which beta-blocker therapy is contraindicated.

- Inability to perform PiCCO® monitoring (e.g., absence of appropriate arterial or central venous access).
